Paper: Deep unsupervised 3D human body reconstruction from a sparse set of landmarks
Section: Introduction

Reconstruction of 3D human body has a great applicability in many domains including pose and shape retargeting, movie editing, videogame industry and virtual reality, just to name a few. This is a particularly challenging problem, since the solution must deal with 3D joint locations and orientations along with subject specific body surface. Besides, data acquisition and annotation is an expensive process, specially for supervised approaches.Given the difficulty of acquiring 3D ground truth body surface, this problem is tackled unsupervisedly in different ways in the literature. On the one hand, image-based approaches , try to reconstruct 3D body from 2D data gathered from images. However, this is known as ill-posed since depth is lost in the projection to the image plane and 2D-to-3D reconstruction can have multiple solutions for the same 2D data. Some authors propose multi-camera setups, to cope with this problem. On the other hand, mocap-based pose estimation has become a standard procedure in domain specific applications like movie and videogame industry. However, standard procedures are not able to reconstruct body surface. In this regard, Loper etal. showed that a sparse set of physical landmarks attached to the body is enough to reconstruct the whole body surface.In this paper we focus on mocap-based solutions. Prior works , are based on regular optimization techniques in which a statistical body model is fit to the input landmarks. These approaches are able to reconstruct the body surface accurately, though, in a significant amount of time. Besides, optimization is applied in several steps, e.g., body shape is optimized first and later pose is conditioned on shape. This further prevents these approaches to be utilized in on-the-fly applications. On the contrary, in this paper we propose a deep unsupervised approach to reconstruct 3D body surface from single frame mocap data which is fast in training and testing time, able to generate accurate results. Working on single frames, rather than sequences, relaxes the network from the need of enormous temporal data, allowing our approach to be trained on small custom datasets. To the best of our knowledge this is the first time a deep unsupervised approach is applied to this problem.Specifically, we build our approach based on a widely used statistical generative model (SMPL) . SMPL receives body pose and shape parameters, updates a template mesh and generates body surface through forward kinematic. The goal of this paper is to estimate SMPL pose and shape parameters from mocap data through deep learning such that generated surface best fits the input 3D landmarks. There are several challenges in this task: 1) landmarks are noisy and sometimes missing, 2) although SMPL is differentiable, it is sensitive to noise, and 3) the space of human pose and shape is highly non-linear. These challenges produce many local minima and an efficient architecture and training procedure are crucial for model generalization. Given the aforementioned challenges, one goal in this paper is to design a network that can work well in small size custom datasets.We inspire our architecture from SMPLR , in which a set of landmarks are predicted from input RGB images and used to estimate body pose and shape. SMPLR is a supervised approach which is not applicable on the problem at hand. Our main contribution is to redesign SMPLR for unsupervised training. Specifically, our contributions are as follows. Our proposed architecture is composed of a denoising autoencoder (similar to SMPLR) to recover missing landmarks, an attention model to estimate joints from landmarks, and a cascading regression model to estimate body pose and shape parameters. We train the model unsupervisedly, that is, 3D joints and body pose and shape parameters are unknown.

Section: Introduction

State-of-the-art methods that estimate 3D body pose and shape given an image, or a video , have recently shown impressive results. A major challenge when training models for in-the-wild human pose estimation is data: collecting large sets of training images with ground-truth 3D annotations is cumbersome as it requires setting up IMUs , calibrating a multi-camera system  or considering static poses .
In practice, only 2D information such as 2D keypoint locations or semantic part segmentation can be manually annotated.
Current methods therefore leverage this in-the-wild data with partial ground-truth annotations by defining their losses on the 2D reprojection of the 3D estimation , by running an optimization-based method  beforehand and curate the obtained ground-truth  or by running the optimization inside the training loop .

Recently, several of these MoCap datasets have been unified into the large AMASS dataset . Importantly, all the considered MoCap sequences were converted into realistic 3D human meshes represented by a rigged body model, concretely SMPL , a differentiable parametric model employed by most state-of-the-art human mesh recovery methods, .

In this case, these data are only used to force the model to predict a realistic output, without improving its capability to better estimate the poses by seeing more diverse examples. manageable description. But as soon as an approximation is done, the resulting

phenomenological equations at the Hilbert space level, an approach which is useful

expected_output: Betti curves of random symmetric matrices and geometric ones exhibit distinct topological features due to the differences in their underlying structures. Random symmetric matrices have Betti curves that are consistent and similar in organization, indicating that most matrix orderings have a similar arrangement of cliques. In contrast, geometric matrices, which are obtained as the distance matrix of sample points randomly distributed on a manifold, have Betti curves that are dramatically different due to the non-uniform sampling of possible matrix orderings. The computational complexity of calculating Betti curves for random symmetric matrices is generally lower than for geometric matrices, as the former can be generated and analyzed more straightforwardly. However, the topological features of geometric matrices, such as those derived from Euclidean, spherical, or hyperbolic spaces, can provide valuable insights into the underlying geometric properties of the data, making their computation worthwhile despite the increased complexity. expected_output: To ensure compliance with multiple regulatory frameworks, such as EU GDPR, US HIPAA, and US FISMA, in a unified approach to data protection, it is essential to establish a comprehensive framework that addresses the requirements of each regulation. This can be achieved by setting guidelines and regulations that define transparent and fair data collection, as seen in the General Data Protection Regulation in Europe and the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act in the US. Additionally, implementing a hierarchical cybersecurity model, such as the one suggested by Strielkina et al. for healthcare IoT systems, can help encompass relationships between different regulations and provide tool support for corresponding decision-making. Furthermore, using multiple regulations to extract penalty clauses and train machine learning models for automated identification and deconstruction of penalty clauses, as done by Anish et al., can also be an effective approach. Ultimately, a unified approach to data protection requires a thorough understanding of the regulatory landscape and the implementation of best practices and standards that cater to the specific needs of healthcare organizations and public administrations.
actual_output: To ensure compliance with multiple regulatory frameworks, such as EU GDPR, US HIPAA, and US FISMA, in a unified approach to data protection, it is essential to understand the specific guidelines and standards set by each regulation [1][2]. The GDPR, for instance, sets strict guidelines for the collection, processing, storage, and transfer of personal data, which is defined broadly to include information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, and requires explicit and verifiable consent from data subjects [1][3][4]. HIPAA, on the other hand, establishes standards and safeguards for the protection of sensitive patient health information, known as Protected Health Information (PHI), and outlines the standards for protecting individuals' medical records and other personal health information held by covered entities and their business associates [2]. By harmonizing data protection laws and adhering to the principles of each regulation, organizations can develop a unified approach to data protection that ensures compliance with multiple regulatory frameworks [5].

It outlines standards and safeguards for covered entities, such as healthcare providers and health plans, that must be followed to secure ePHI. The rule encompasses administrative, physical, and technical safeguards, requiring entities to implement policies, procedures, and technologies to safeguard electronic health information's confidentiality, integrity, and availability.The HIPAA Omnibus Rule introduced significant modifications to strengthen the HIPAA policy. Additionally, it incorporated amendments related to the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA), further safeguarding genetic information from misuse in health plans.The HIPAA Breach Notification Rule mandates that covered entities and their business associates notify affected individuals, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and, in certain cases, the media in case of a breach of protected health information (PHI). expected_output: The construction of the CKM matrix at tree-level and the unitarity triangle approach differ in their methods to achieve precise CP violation measurements. The tree-level construction of the CKM matrix utilizes the measured values of the CKM elements, while the unitarity triangle approach employs the unitarity of the CKM matrix to constrain the parameters. In terms of CP implications, the tree-level construction is sensitive to the CP violating phase, and the unitarity triangle approach provides a framework to estimate the likely presence of CP violation in the leptonic sector. The main difference between the two approaches lies in their treatment of theoretical inputs and experimental errors, with the tree-level construction being more susceptible to New Physics effects and the unitarity triangle approach providing a more robust framework for precision measurements. Overall, both approaches are essential for understanding the CKM phenomenology and achieving precise CP violation measurements, with the unitarity triangle approach offering a more comprehensive framework for analyzing the CP implications.

Direct measurements of sin(2beta) and cos(2beta) alone are sufficient to constrain the unitarity triangle to a precision of about 10%, constituting a precision test of the CKM picture of CP violation in B meson decays [3]. input: What are the limitations of using auto-fit isochrones in determining age accuracy, and how do different methodologies impact the overall precision of age estimates?
expected_output: The use of auto-fit isochrones in determining age accuracy has several limitations, including the potential for stochastic effects, large color dispersion at fainter magnitudes, and photometry incompleteness at the bottom part of the color-magnitude diagrams (CMDs). Additionally, residuals from field star decontamination can also impact the accuracy of age estimates. The automatic technique used by B17 to fit isochrones to the observed CMDs may have left little space to control these effects, which could have resulted in inaccurate age estimates, particularly for older clusters. Furthermore, the presence of residual LMC red clump stars, in combination with relatively faint main sequences, could mimic the appearance of features typically seen in CMDs of clusters older than log(8.7) years, leading to incorrect age estimates. Different methodologies, such as the use of nominal reddenings and the selection of isochrones, can also impact the overall precision of age estimates, highlighting the need for careful consideration of these factors in determining the ages of star clusters.
actual_output: The limitations of using auto-fit isochrones in determining age accuracy include reliance on specific physics in theoretical models and the fitting technique itself, as there are two major drawbacks to fitting isochrones [1]. A significant problem in using isochrones is that they are not evenly spaced in the HRD, leading to biased results, which can impact the overall precision of age estimates [2]. Different methodologies, such as applying various data augmentation techniques, can influence the model performance, and increasing the data amount consistently improves model accuracy on both young and old populations [3]. Isochrone fitting methods constitute a 'hybrid' of sorts between vertical and horizontal methods, using both magnitudes and colors as age diagnostics, but are generally considered suitable for the determination of relative ages only [4].

Paper: An empirical isochrone archive for nearby open clusters
Section: Introduction

Since there is no measurable parameter that enables unequivocal age determination, various methods have been developed to estimate stellar population ages using different indicators. These include asteroseismology , evaporation ages , gyrochronology, kinematic and traceback ages, lithium depletion (boundary) measurements, or lithium equivalent widths . However, these methods all share a “specialist” limitation, in that they may only be suited for specific age, temperature, or mass ranges, require precise, work-intensive observed parameters, or can only be applied to either individual stars or ensembles. .Contrasting these rather specialized methods with narrow application ranges is an approach often praised for its generalistic nature – isochrone fitting. Based on variants of the Hertzsprung-Russel diagram, particularly the color-absolute magnitude diagram (CMD), it is a popular estimation technique with only minimal observational data requirements. As a result of Gaia providing photometry and astrometry for billions of sources, isochrone fitting has become perhaps the most used approach to age determination to date. Because of its connection to the HRD, the method is widely applicable across stellar age and mass ranges, for example from 0.5 Myr to 10 Gyr for M_* = 0.01 - 1.4~M_{\odot } or 10 Myr to 12.5 Gyr for M_* = 0.09 - 14~M_{\odot } . There are two major drawbacks to fitting isochrones, though: On the one hand, it heavily relies on the specific physics considered when modeling the theoretical isochrones. As the different physical processes of stellar evolution are highly complex and vary between different stellar ages and masses , this translates into a large number of free parameters, which can produce systematic errors in age estimates across different stellar evolution models and prior assumptions. Given the many different available stellar evolution codes for model isochrones, such as BHAC15 , DSEP-magnetic , BT-Settl , PARSEC, MIST , and BaSTI, this dependence has a profound impact on age estimates found in literature. On the other hand, the fitting technique of the isochrones to the CMD data itself can strongly impact the results. From the observational side, measurement errors and incomplete or contaminated cluster member data are drivers of age uncertainties .Additionally, observational cluster CMDs include an unknown amount of unresolved binary stars. The extent of this contaminating population has been estimated to range from about 29 to 50 % , and equal mass unresolved binaries reside at the maximum possible displacement of -0.753mag above the main sequence. Additionally, reddening effects of non-equal mass unresolved binaries have been found to cause a shift of the corresponding data points closer, or right onto, the equal mass binary sequence , . expected_output: Isolation measures have been shown to reduce COVID-19 transmission rates in densely populated areas. input: What causes PMMH log-likelihood variance to exceed 1 in certain models, and how do different methodologies contribute to this phenomenon?
expected_output: The PMMH log-likelihood variance exceeds 1 in certain models due to the sensitivity of the PMMH method to the size of the variance of the log of the estimated likelihood. In many problems, it is computationally demanding to ensure that the variance of the log of the estimated likelihood is around 1, which can lead to a deterioration in the performance of the PMMH method. The use of a large number of particles, such as 2000, can help to obtain an unbiased estimate of the likelihood, but this can be computationally expensive. The correlated PMMH approach, which correlates the pseudo-random numbers used in estimating the likelihood at the current and proposed values of the Markov chain, can help to reduce the variance of the log-likelihood and improve the performance of the PMMH method. Additionally, the use of different methodologies, such as the AISIL-PG and AISIL-HMC methods, can also contribute to the phenomenon of exceeding 1, as these methods may require more tuning and can be more sensitive to the choice of parameters, such as the number of particles and leapfrog steps.
actual_output: The variance of the PMMH log-likelihood can exceed 1 due to various factors, including the number of observations and the dimension of the latent states, as the variance of the log of the estimated likelihood grows with these parameters [1]. In idealized conditions, the variance of the log of the estimated likelihood should be around 1 for optimal PMMH performance, but in practice, controlling the variance of the difference in the log likelihood estimates at current and proposed values is crucial for PMMH efficiency [2][3]. Different methodologies, such as the correlated PMMH approach, can reduce the variance of the log of the estimated likelihood by correlating pseudo-random numbers used in estimating the likelihood at current and proposed values, and the number of particles used in the particle filter can be chosen to balance computational time and MCMC mixing, with a target variance range of 1 to 3 [2][1]. Increasing the number of particles in the particle filter can decrease the variance of the log of the ratio of the likelihood estimates, and optimal performance for random walk proposals in PMMH is achieved when the standard deviation of the estimated log-likelihood is between 1 and 2 [4].

The context highlights the challenges of adapting object detection models to fisheye imagery due to the oriented and radially distorted objects, and explores alternative representations for standard bounding boxes to improve accuracy. In terms of key differences in performance, fisheye cameras are shown to require specialized models and techniques, such as curved boxes, oriented boxes, ellipses, and polygons, to achieve reasonable tradeoffs between model complexity and accuracy. Additionally, the context notes that the performance of fisheye cameras can be improved by incorporating geometric priors into the loss function and using vehicle motion awareness, but a direct comparison to pinhole cameras in various lighting conditions is not provided. Cross-device visual positioning presents significant challenges for IR, local matching, and APRs. Our VC1 and VC2 methods demonstrate practical enhancements in the performance of IR and APR for cross-device scenarios. However, it is essential to note that during the local matching process, the accuracy of matches and the recall and precision of IR for query frames from different cameras may not align perfectly. The chosen IR method and its training noticeably affect accuracy for similar cameras. Fisheye cameras exhibit better performance in IR compared to pinhole cameras. However, pinhole cameras outperform fisheye cameras for high accuracy and median accuracy levels in local matching. This is likely due to existing feature extraction and matching models lacking training data on 360^\circ and fisheye cameras, resulting in less accurate matching. We attribute the inferior performance of pinhole query frames at the low accuracy level to IR's insufficient recall and precision.
Additionally, pinhole queries are more susceptible to interference when there are many
repetitive and symmetrical features in the scene, even when the retrieved reference image is correct (some example figures in the supplementary material).
By utilizing VC2 to augment IR and APR's training data, we eliminate the cross-device domain gap. We demonstrate that panoramic perspective and a larger FoV can significantly improve the performance of IR and APRs and find that query frames from 360^\circ camera and ultra-wide FoV cameras are less prone to being misidentified as erroneous locations with similar structures. This finding indicates that fisheye cameras and 360^\circ cameras hold great promise as sensors in indoor environments with low GPS accuracy for localization tasks.

The first successful commercial application of fisheye cameras was in photography, particularly in the entertainment industry, where the fisheye lens effect became a stylistic element. A video by Vox provides an excellent overview of the history of its usage. The second successful area of application is video surveillance, where the hemispherical lens surface can be commonly seen in modern surveillance systems . More recently, wide-angle lens cameras are commonly used in virtual reality headsets . They are also commonly used in underwater robotics , and aerial robotics .Automotive is one of the important application areas of fisheye cameras where more advanced visual perception is necessary.
The first wide-angle rear-view camera and a TV display were deployed in General Motors' Buick Centurion concept model in 1956. In 2018, a rear-view fisheye camera was mandated in the United States to reduce accidents during reversing . In 2008, surround-view cameras were deployed by BMW for park view . Surround-view cameras have become a commonly used feature in many vehicles. They were subsequently used for computer vision applications like cross-traffic alerts , object detection , and automated parking . The addition of a fisheye lens dramatically increases the field-of-view to 190 ∘ 190^\circ due to refraction. (bottom) Refraction of light rays at the surface of water causes compression of the horizon into a smaller field-of-view.]Fisheye cameras have several challenges, however. The most obvious is that they exhibit a strong radial distortion that cannot be corrected without disadvantages, including reduced field-of-view and resampling distortion artifacts at the periphery . Appearance variations of objects are larger due to the spatially variant distortion, particularly for close-by objects. This increases the learning complexity of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), which uses translation invariance as an inductive bias and increases sample complexity as the model has to learn the appearance of all the distorted versions of an object. In addition, the commonly used application of object detection using a bounding box becomes more complex as the bounding box does not provide an optimal fit for fisheye distorted objects, as illustrated in Figure REF . More sophisticated representations instead of a rectangular box, such as a curved bounding box exploiting the known radial distortion of fisheye cameras, were explored in . Fisheye perception is a challenging task, and despite its prevalence, it is comparatively less explored than pinhole cameras.In the case of cameras without significant fisheye distortion, there is a very common geometry associated with them, being the pinhole model. One may first consider the intersection of a ray with a single planar surface at some fixed distance from the projection center. All models of the distortion due to the lens for such cameras then are simply designed to shift the intersection point position radially from the projection center on the plane. In a way, fisheye algorithm development has been complicated by the lack of a unifying geometry. Many models use different properties to describe fisheye projection.

Paper: Near-field Perception for Low-Speed Vehicle Automation using Surround-view Fisheye Cameras
Section: Introduction

Fisheye cameras offer a distinct advantage for automotive applications. Given their extremely wide field of view, they can observe the full surrounding of a vehicle with a minimal number of sensors.
Typically four cameras is all that is required for full 360[FORMULA] coverage of a car (Figure REF ).
However, this advantage comes with a cost given the significantly more complex projection geometry. Several papers in the past have provided reviews of how to model fisheye geometry, e.g., . We do not aim to repeat this here and will rather focus on the problems that the use of fisheye camera technology brings to automotive visual perception.In standard field of view cameras, the principles of rectilinear projection and perspective are closely approximated, with the usual perspective properties, i.e., straight lines in the real world are projected as straight lines on the image plane. Parallel sets of straight lines are projected as a set of lines that are convergent on a single vanishing point on the image plane. Deviations from this through optical distortions are easily corrected. Many automotive datasets provide image data with optical distortions removed , with an easy means for correction , or with almost imperceptible optical distortion . As such, most research in automotive vision makes an implicit assumption of rectilinear projection. Fish-eye perspective differs significantly from rectilinear perspective. A straight line in the camera scene is projected as a curved line on the fish-eye image plane, and parallel sets of lines are projected as a set of curves that converge at two vanishing points . This distortion is immediately obvious in the examples presented in this paper (e.g., Figures REF , REF and REF ). However, distortion is not the only effect. Figure REF shows an image from a typical mirror mounted camera in a surround-view system. In a fisheye camera, the orientation in the image of objects depends on their location in the image. In this example, the vehicle on the left is rotated almost 90[FORMULA] compared to the vehicle on the right. This has an impact on the translation invariance assumed in convolutional approaches to object detection. In standard cameras, translation invariance is an acceptable assumption. However, this is not the case in fisheye imagery, as evidenced in Figure REF . One must carefully consider how to handle this in any computer vision algorithm design.
[Figure: Significant deviation from translation invariance is evident in fisheye cameras.]A natural approach to address these issues is to rectify the images in some manner. We can immediately discard rectifying to a single planar image, as firstly, too much of the field of view would necessarily be lost thus negating the advantage of fisheye imagery and secondly interpolation and perspective artefacts would quickly dominate the rectified output. A common approach is use multi-planar rectification, whereby different portions of the fisheye image are warped to different planar images. For example, we can define a cube, and warp the image on to the surfaces of the cube. Figure REF shows warpings on to two such surfaces. Even here, interpolation and perspective effects are visible, and one must deal with the complexity of surface transitions. Another rectification approach is to consider warping to a cylindrical surface, as per Figure REF . In such a warping, the axis of the cylinder is configured such that it is vertical to the ground. The observation is that most objects of interest in an automotive scene lie and move on an approximately horizontal plane, being the road surface.

input: What is the process for adapting TTRS to open-source software, and how can TTRC's approach be applied to achieve this adaptation?
expected_output: The process for adapting Time To Restore Service (TTRS) to open-source software involves modifying the metric to Time To Repair Code (TTRC), which measures the time it takes to release a new version of the code that includes changes that correct bugs. To achieve this adaptation, the TTRC approach can be applied by calculating the time difference between the moment a bug issue is raised and the moment the changes that solve the bug are released in a new version of the code. This is done by defining a formula that sums up the time differences for each bug and then dividing by the total number of bugs reported during a period of time. The result is the mean time to repair code, which can be used to evaluate the stability of open-source software projects. Additionally, the standard deviation of the time to repair code can be calculated to reflect the variations in the time it takes to solve different bugs, providing further insight into the project's stability.
actual_output: The process for adapting TTRS to open-source software involves test-time adaptation methods, such as Test-time Adaptation (TTA), which aims to reconcile the distribution shifts in an online manner [1]. TCR, a novel method for test-time adaptation in cross-modal retrieval under query shift, can be applied to achieve this adaptation by first employing a novel module to refine the query predictions and then adopting a novel joint objective to prevent the model adaptation from overfitting noise [2][3]. This joint objective manipulates the intra-modality uniformity and inter-modality gap to preserve the well-established common space from the source model, which is crucial for adapting TTRS to open-source software [3].

Paper: Test-time Adaptation for Cross-modal Retrieval with Query Shift
Section: Discussion

In this paper, we develop a new test-time adaptation method, dubbed TCR, to achieve robust cross-modal retrieval against the query shift problem.
In brief, TCR first employs a novel module to refine the query predictions.
After that, TCR adopts a novel joint objective to prevent the model adaptation from overfitting noise while simultaneously manipulating the intra-modality uniformity and inter-modality gap to preserve the well-established common space from the source model.
Extensive experiments not only verify the effectiveness of TCR but also reveal the importance of each designs.
In the future, we plan to explore more potential scenarios contaminated with query shift and extend TCR to address the corresponding issues.Appendix.tocmtappendix

Paper: Test-time Adaptation for Cross-modal Retrieval with Query Shift
Section: Introduction

Test-time Adaptation (TTA) has emerged as a promising avenue for domain adaptation, which aims to reconcile the distribution shifts in an online manner.
Towards achieving this goal, some Test-Time Training (TTT) approaches, have been proposed, which require modifying the training process of the source model and adding an auxiliary self-supervised task.
As a result, the source model could be adapted by performing the self-supervised task on the online target data stream.
To avoid the reduplicated training cost of the source model, Fully Test-Time Adaptation  paradigm has been proposed, which could be coarsely divided into the following three categories: i) online TTA methods, which continually update the normalization layers by resorting to the unsupervised objectives, such as entropy minimization or its variants. ii) robust TTA methods, which strive to improve the robustness against noisy predictions, mixed distribution shifts, label shifts, and so on. iii) TTA beyond recognition, which focuses on the tasks including but not limited to image restoration , multimodal recognition , and multimodal segmentation .In this paper, we focus on online TTA for achieving robust cross-modal retrieval against query shift.

input: How does Gini impurity compare to Entropy impurity in terms of their effectiveness in decision tree splitting across different datasets and algorithms?
expected_output: Gini impurity and Entropy impurity are two of the most commonly used impurity measures in decision tree splitting, and their effectiveness can vary across different datasets and algorithms. In general, both measures are effective in guiding the decision tree splitting process, but they have different properties that can make one more suitable than the other in certain situations. The Gini impurity measure is used in the CART package, while the Entropy impurity measure is used in the C4.5 decision tree inducer. Research has shown that the choice of impurity measure can affect the performance of the decision tree, with some studies suggesting that Entropy impurity can lead to more accurate classifications, while others have found that Gini impurity can result in more efficient tree construction. Ultimately, the choice of impurity measure depends on the specific characteristics of the dataset and the goals of the analysis.

In comparison, Entropy impurity, also known as Shannon Entropy, is another function used to judge the quality of split in decision trees, measuring the disorder in the information content and the unpredictability in a particular node [3]. Both Gini impurity and Entropy impurity are used to minimize node impurity and increase homogeneity of class labels, but the choice between them may depend on the specific dataset and algorithm, with Gini impurity being used in decision tree splitting to select the split that maximizes the reduction in impurity using a greedy approach [4][5]. While the Gini index is specifically used as the impurity measurement for decision tree splitting, Entropy measures the unpredictability in the information contained in a node, and the decision on when to split in the tree can be decided using either method, depending on the context [6][7].

Section: Introduction

Machine learning (ML) methods often aid the analysis of the vast amounts of data that are produced by contemporary high energy physics (HEP) experiments.
The ML algorithms often feature tunable parameters, referred to as hyperparameters, which need to be chosen by the user and often have a significant effect on the algorithm's performance.
In a previous publication  we presented two different algorithms, particle swarm optimisation (PSO) and the genetic algorithm, for the autonomous determination of these hyperparameters.
In the present paper we compare the performance of the PSO algorithm, the more promising of the two algorithms studied in our previous publication, to the performance of the Bayesian optimisation (BO), algorithm. The latter is widely used for the task of finding optimal hyperparameter values in the context of ML applications since the pioneering work of Refs., .
The “asynchronous successive halving algorithm” (ASHA)  is an alternative
algorithm for optimising the values of hyperparameters, which is popular in the ML community outside the field of HEP.As in our previous publication, we formulate the task of determining the set of optimal hyperparameter values as a function maximisation problem.

We compare the performance of the PSO and BO algorithms on two benchmark tasks,
the task of finding the minimum of the Rosenbrock function ,
and on a typical data analysis task in the field of HEP, the “ATLAS Higgs boson machine learning challenge” .An important aspect in applications of ML algorithms in the field of HEP is an algorithm's capability to make efficient use of massively parallel computing facilities.
A single training of an ML algorithm on a single machine may take several hours, days, or, in extreme cases, even weeks.

However, we did not explicitly perform fine-tuning for the hyperparameters of the AutoML toolbox methods. Some conventional methods from the AutoML toolbox may be affected by the number of observations and classes. For instance, the training time of one vs one SVM is quadratic proportional to the number of classes because each binary classifier is trained on a pair of classes, requiring a number of binary classifiers equal to the number of pairs of classes. This number grows quadratically with the number of classes, with N(N-1)/2 pairs of classes for N classes. Paper: Hybrid Unsupervised Learning Strategy for Monitoring Industrial Batch Processes
Section: Introduction

Continuous monitoring of complex manufacturing processes involves the systematic surveillance, measurement, and analysis of various aspects of a production system to ensure efficient operation, maintain product quality, and comply with safety standards. Anomaly detection is a critical aspect of a comprehensive monitoring system and involves the identification of atypical patterns, events, or behaviors in datasets that significantly deviate from the norm or expected values. In the domain of manufacturing processes, multivariate datasets encompass correlated time-sequenced records of process values. Multivariate anomaly detection techniques can be divided into two main categories: statistical and machine learning (ML) methods (). While production processes are characterized by high system order with complex interactions between multiple process values, machine learning (ML) methods are preferred - they can effectively learn and model complex, non-linear relationships (). Supervised ML methods require labeled training data (e.g., normal or abnormal behavior), while unsupervised methods do not. Unsupervised ML methods assume that the recorded data reflects the normal behavior of the process, thus reducing the cost of data preparation and labeling. Clustering-based ML techniques group similar data points into clusters - anomaly is measured by how well a data point fits into the identified clusters. An additional layer of analysis is added by interpreting the clusters as characteristic phases of a process (e.g., start, steady, transient, end). This can be useful when monitoring batch processes in the pharmaceutical industry, for example, where the duration and sequence of process phases (phase trajectory) are critical in terms of product quality. Self-organizing maps (SOMs), introduced by , have been successfully employed for process monitoring in various applications. While the approaches presented in , focus on anomaly detection, the concepts presented in , extend the utility of SOMs to identify, visualize, and monitor process phases. However, SOMs have certain limitations, especially when dealing with unbalanced training datasets and highly correlated process variables. To overcome these problems, a hybrid unsupervised learning strategy (HULS) have been presented by . In order to evaluate the performance of the developed method, a comparative study based on a synthetic dataset was conducted. The experiments showed that the HULS concept is significantly superior, especially in the reliable identification of unknown process phases.
In this study, we explore the use of the HULS procedure for monitoring a laboratory batch process. Section  outlines the basic methods used, while Section  gives an overview of the HULS approach. Section  presents the experimental results, comparing the performance of HULS with SOM method. Finally, the paper is concluded in Section .

We present new constraints on the relationship between galaxies and their
host dark matter halos, measured from the location of the peak of the
stellar-to-halo mass ratio (SHMR), up to the most massive galaxy clusters at
redshift $z\sim0.8$ and over a volume of nearly 0.1~Gpc$^3$. We use a unique
combination of deep observations in the CFHTLenS/VIPERS field from the near-UV
to the near-IR, supplemented by $\sim60\,000$ secure spectroscopic redshifts,
analysing galaxy clustering, galaxy-galaxy lensing and the stellar mass
function. We interpret our measurements within the halo occupation distribution
(HOD) framework, separating the contributions from central and satellite
galaxies. We find that the SHMR for the central galaxies peaks at $M_{\rm h,
peak} = 1.9^{+0.2}_{-0.1}\times10^{12} M_{\odot}$ with an amplitude of $0.025$,
which decreases to $\sim0.001$ for massive halos ($M_{\rm h} > 10^{14}
M_{\odot}$). Compared to central galaxies only, the total SHMR (including
satellites) is boosted by a factor 10 in the high-mass regime (cluster-size
halos), a result consistent with cluster analyses from the literature based on
fully independent methods. After properly accounting for differences in
modelling, we have compared our results with a large number of results from the
literature up to $z=1$: we find good general agreement, independently of the
method used, within the typical stellar-mass systematic errors at low to
intermediate mass (${M}_{\star} < 10^{11} M_{\odot}$) and the statistical
errors above. We have also compared our SHMR results to semi-analytic
simulations and found that the SHMR is tilted compared to our measurements in
such a way that they over- (under-) predict star formation efficiency in
central (satellite) galaxies.

input: What are the limitations of using cogenerating subcategories and exact functors in assessing cotorsion, and how do their interactions impact the overall effectiveness of this approach in practice?
expected_output: The limitations of using cogenerating subcategories and exact functors in assessing cotorsion lie in the requirement that the subcategory must be closed under countable products and the functors must be exact, which may not always be the case in practice. Additionally, the approach relies on the existence of enough injective objects in the category, which is not guaranteed. The interactions between cogenerating subcategories and exact functors can impact the effectiveness of this approach, as the closure of the subcategory under countable products and the exactness of the functors are crucial in ensuring that the quasi-isomorphism between complexes exists. Furthermore, the fact that the class of cotorsion contramodules is usually not generating in the category of contramodules can limit the applicability of this approach. However, as shown in Proposition 12.6, if the subcategory is cogenerating and closed under countable products, and the functors are exact, then for any complex in the category, there exists a quasi-isomorphism to a complex in the subcategory, which can be useful in practice. Overall, the effectiveness of this approach depends on the specific category and subcategory being considered, and careful analysis of the limitations and interactions is necessary to ensure its successful application.

Furthermore, an exact functor between triangulated categories preserves all products if and only if it has a left adjoint, which is a crucial property for assessing cotorsion, and this is closely related to the concept of a functor being cogenerating if and only if the unit of the adjunction is a monomorphism [2][3]. Section: Methods

The Moving-MNIST dataset has been a common benchmark to evaluate how well a model could predict motion in spatial preservation and temporal extrapolation. However, the nature of the Moving-MNIST is highly deterministic, which does not resemble the chaotic nature of the atmospheric system. Previous adaptations attempted to simulate the physical dynamics by introducing a set of complex motions such as rotation and scaling or by applying an external force on collision . We argue that the fundamental reason causing the blur in precipitation nowcasting is the intrinsic stochasticity of the motion caused by external factors unseen in the weather dataset, such as orographic effects, vertical wind shear, interaction with other weather systems, etc. Trained with such stochasticity, regular models with pixel-wise loss could consistently fail to provide quality prediction in the future lead time.To verify our claim, we introduce a simplistic modification to the Moving-MNIST dataset. The standard Moving-MNIST dataset contains handwritten digits sampled from the MNIST dataset moving and bouncing with a constant velocity (u_0, v_0) on the 64\times 64 image plane. To introduce stochasticity, we perturb the velocity with a random Gaussian noise \epsilon at each time step. Details of the perturbation are shown in Appendix . In the upcoming sections, we dub this dataset Stochastic Moving-MNIST and apply the experimental setting to this synthetic dataset. The performance of combinations of different losses and models can be found in Table REF and qualitative visualizations of the corresponding methods are shown in Figure REF and Appendix . Note that the Stochastic Moving-MNIST is used in both training and evaluation to ensure that the models are well exposed to motion randomness.

From top to bottom: Input, Ground Truth, MSE, FACL.]In Table REF , our modification drastically improves the sharpness and realisticity for all tested models, as reflected by the vast reduction in LPIPS and RHD. In particular, FACL reduces up to 57\% of LPIPS and 71\% of RHD for the ConvLSTM model. The pixel-wise and structural metrics between the two losses are comparable. On the other hand, generative models result in much poorer MAE and SSIM, with skill scores like FSS still being worse than most of the baseline models. In Figure REF , we can observe that the model trained with MSE cannot reconstruct a clear spatial pattern, especially in the subsequent frames, while the model trained with FACL yields much sharper and higher quality outputs. Consequently, we can conclude that in this setting with the synthetic Stochastic Moving-MNIST, FACL demonstrates a significant improvement in perceptual metrics and skill scores, with the quality on par with that of generative models.

Paper: CorrectBench: Automatic Testbench Generation with Functional Self-Correction using LLMs for HDL Design
Section: Introduction

Simulation-based functional verification, relying on a testbench (TB), is among the most prevalent verification techniques employed during the initial phases of hardware design. The engineering effort required to design a testbench for functional simulation remains significantly high , with much of this effort being task-specific. This specificity complicates finding a generic method to optimize the process.
Previous works, such as those by, have primarily focused on automating the generation of test stimuli for the design under test (DUT), which constitutes the front end of the functional simulation. The back end involves verifying the correctness of the signals from the DUT, which is highly specialized, making traditional automation methods ineffective and thus unattainable for the fully automated testbench design.The increasing application of LLMs in the digital hardware design process suggests an alternative approach to automating testbench design. Recent studies, demonstrated the effectiveness of LLMs in various aspects of hardware design, particularly in Register-transfer level (RTL) design.
Some research efforts have extended beyond basic RTL design correction using LLMs , . In the realm of functional simulation-based verification, preliminary efforts have been made.
For instance, investigates the potential of LLMs in generating testbenches for finite state machines (FSMs), while introduces a framework called AutoBench, the first systematic and generic testbench generation framework.
Although achieving an average 57% improvement compared with directly generating testbench using LLMs, AutoBench still suffers from a low success rate. This limitation arises from the inherent uncertainty of LLMs, such as hallucination and laziness . Additionally, AutoBench employs only syntax self-checking, similar to RTLFixer , without implementing functional self-checking. This is a common issue in current LLM-based hardware design methodologies, the absence of a self-checking mechanism indeed limits the potential performance of the AutoBench framework.
[Figure: The outline of CorrectBench workflow.]To address the aforementioned issues, this paper proposes CorrectBench, the first framework for automatic testbench generation that incorporates functional self-validation and self-correction. Our framework utilizes the design specification (SPEC) of the device under test (DUT) in natural language as the sole input, as illustrated in Fig. REF , while expanding the boundaries of current testbench generation methods.
The contributions of this work are summarized as follows:An action-based testbench self-validation and self-correction framework is proposed. The total testbench generation pass ratio is improved up to 70.13%, compared with 52.18% in the previous work and 33.33% in a direct method where LLMs are applied directly to generate test benches. Specifically in sequential circuits, our work's performance is 62.18% higher than previous work in sequential tasks and almost 5 times the direct method.

A scenario-based testbench self-validator is proposed, validating the correctness of the generated testbench via a particular matrix. The validator only takes the task specification in natural language as the input information and achieves an average 88.85% validation accuracy.

An LLM-based testbench self-corrector is used to take the bug information from the validator as the input. The corrector makes a 34.33% contribution in the total improvement compared with previous work.

The code, dataset, and experimental results are open-sourced on https://github.com/AutoBench/CorrectBench.

Paper: AutoBench: Automatic Testbench Generation and Evaluation Using LLMs for HDL Design
Section: Discussion

LLMs still encounter challenges such as laziness , hallucination and insufficient training data on hardware design, making the direct generation of testbenches for complex DUTs ineffective.
For instance, due to LLM laziness, the generated testbench may end prematurely after listing only a few test cases, resulting in low coverage.
Additionally, the reference signals required to verify the DUT are not always clear from DUT's specification.
In complex cases, context-based LLMs may guess incorrect values due to hallucination.
Furthermore, commercial LLMs such as GPT-4 Turbo are trained more extensively on software codes than hardware codes, indicating a weak performance in hardware contexts.
To address issues of laziness and hallucination, AutoBench divides the testbench generation process into multiple stages, applying the idea of chain-of-thought .
Additionally, our hybrid testbench structure uses software code, leveraging the advantage of more comprehensive training data in the software domain for a better performance.

input: How does the PS condition contribute to ensuring sequence convergence, and what are the key properties that make it effective across different mathematical frameworks?
expected_output: The Palais-Smale (PS) condition plays a crucial role in ensuring sequence convergence by providing a framework for establishing the existence of convergent subsequences in various mathematical contexts. In the context of functional analysis and optimization, the PS condition ensures that a sequence of approximate critical points of a functional converges to a genuine critical point. This is achieved by requiring that any sequence satisfying certain conditions, such as boundedness and gradient convergence, has a convergent subsequence. The key properties that make the PS condition effective include its ability to establish compactness, weak convergence, and strong convergence of sequences, which are essential in a wide range of mathematical frameworks, including calculus of variations, partial differential equations, and optimization theory. By leveraging these properties, the PS condition enables researchers to establish the existence of solutions to various problems, including those involving nonlinear equations and variational inequalities. Furthermore, the PS condition has been adapted and generalized to accommodate different mathematical settings, such as constrained optimization, non-smooth analysis, and infinite-dimensional spaces, making it a fundamental tool in modern mathematics.

input: How does dynamic anisotropy near cut-off frequencies compare to static anisotropy in terms of wave propagation characteristics?
expected_output: Dynamic anisotropy near cut-off frequencies in the context of elastic wave scattering exhibits distinct wave propagation characteristics compared to static anisotropy. In the vicinity of the cut-off frequencies, specifically at ω = √6 for pressure waves and ω = 3√2/2 for shear waves, the dispersion surfaces of the bulk lattice display non-circular slowness contours. These contours lead to preferential directions of wave propagation, resulting in dynamic anisotropy. This phenomenon is manifested in the scattered field through effects such as star-shaped scattered waveforms, negative reflection, and negative refraction. In contrast, static anisotropy refers to the directional dependence of material properties, which can also influence wave propagation. However, dynamic anisotropy near cut-off frequencies is a unique feature that arises from the topology of the dispersion surfaces and is not directly related to static material anisotropy. The dynamic anisotropy observed in this context is a consequence of the frequency-dependent behavior of the lattice, whereas static anisotropy is a property of the material itself, independent of frequency.

Evidence suggests that in the dynamical approach to dislocations, the anisotropy ratio diverges as 1/θ at small polar angles, in contrast to the static approach, where it is formally infinite, further emphasizing the differences between dynamic and static anisotropy [1].

input: How can antiferromagnetic magnon renormalization effects be understood across different filling ranges, and what methods can be employed to analyze these variations?
expected_output: Antiferromagnetic magnon renormalization effects can be understood across different filling ranges by analyzing the behavior of the magnon dispersion relations and the spin stiffness. The renormalization effects become more pronounced at long wavelengths, particularly at the Brillouin zone center, where the spin stiffness decreases with doping and increases with the interaction strength. To analyze these variations, methods such as inelastic neutron scattering (INS) measurements and perturbative expansions can be employed. INS measurements can provide direct information about the magnon dispersion relations, while perturbative expansions can be used to calculate the renormalization effects and the spin stiffness. Additionally, comparisons with experimental results from single crystals of antiferromagnetic heavy fermions, such as CeIn3, can help to validate the theoretical models and provide insight into the behavior of the magnon renormalization effects. By combining these methods, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the antiferromagnetic magnon renormalization effects and their variations across different filling ranges.
actual_output: Antiferromagnetic magnon renormalization effects can be understood across different filling ranges by analyzing how doping away from half-filling results in a smooth reduction of these effects, as expected from the indirect effect which the bare ratio has on magnons [1][2]. Both filling and electron correlation increase renormalization effects in the antiferromagnetic Heisenberg-Kondo model, leading to similar increases of the spin polarization of the conduction band, with the largest renormalization at half-filling due to more conduction electrons contributing through Kondo interaction [2][1]. The renormalization of antiferromagnetic magnons reduces the spin wave frequency with respect to bare magnons, with the effect growing with the bare ratio, and methods such as numerical studies assuming simple cubic interpenetrating magnetic sublattices can be employed to analyze these variations [3][4]. When entering the filling range where the bare electron band develops an itinerant AF polarization, the renormalization effects become much stronger, and the convergence radius of the perturbative series determining magnon renormalization is wider than naively expected, with the actual 'small parameter' being weighed by electronic structure and filling dependent coefficients [5][4].

input: What are the advantages and limitations of using Lagrange multipliers to enhance stability in Stokes equations, and how do different implementations perform in practice across various fluid dynamics applications?
expected_output:
The use of Lagrange multipliers to enhance stability in Stokes equations offers several advantages, including the ability to enforce boundary conditions and improve pressure-robustness, which is essential for accurately simulating fluid dynamics. One of the primary benefits of this approach is that it allows for the creation of a weakly coupled velocity error estimate, where the velocity error's dependence on viscosity is compensated by a higher-order power of the discretization parameter. Additionally, the introduction of Lagrange multipliers can lead to a more stable and optimally convergent method, as demonstrated in the analysis of LBB-unstable and LBB-stable velocity-pressure FE pairs.

However, the implementation of Lagrange multipliers also has some limitations. For instance, the method can be sensitive to the choice of the Lagrange multiplier space and the stabilization technique used. Moreover, the addition of Lagrange multipliers can increase the complexity of the resulting matrices, which can impact the computational efficiency of the method. Different implementations of Lagrange multipliers, such as the Haslinger-Renard method and the Burman-Hansbo method, have been proposed and analyzed, each with its strengths and weaknesses.

In practice, the performance of Lagrange multipliers in enhancing stability in Stokes equations can vary depending on the specific application and the characteristics of the problem. For example, in fluid-structure interaction problems, the use of Lagrange multipliers can be particularly beneficial in handling the complex boundary conditions and the movement of the solid. On the other hand, in problems with complex geometries or high Reynolds numbers, the method may require additional stabilization techniques or modifications to ensure optimal performance.

Overall, the use of Lagrange multipliers to enhance stability in Stokes equations is a powerful tool that can be effective in a wide range of fluid dynamics applications. However, its implementation requires careful consideration of the specific problem characteristics and the choice of the Lagrange multiplier space and stabilization technique. Further research and development are needed to fully explore the potential of this approach and to address the remaining challenges and limitations.

expected_output: The variability of 1665/1667-MHz maser emissions does indeed suggest changes in molecular core conditions, as evidenced by the significant variation in relative amplitudes and velocity components observed across different astronomical observations. The comparison of observed spectra from the VLA and VLBA observations shows good agreement in the central components, but also reveals variability in the intensity of prominent features, such as the 1665 MHz maser lines. Additionally, the shift in velocity scale between the VLA and VLBA observations indicates potential changes in the molecular core conditions. The persistence of multiple 1665-MHz features with considerable variability, as well as the presence of high linear polarization, further supports the notion that changes in molecular core conditions are occurring. Furthermore, the relative proper motions of masers derived from comparing the relative displacement between maser features in different datasets also suggest that the masers are moving at significant tangential velocities, which could be indicative of changes in the molecular core conditions. Overall, the variability of 1665/1667-MHz maser emissions can be consistently observed across different astronomical observations, providing evidence for changes in molecular core conditions.
actual_output: The variability of 1665/1667-MHz maser emissions does indicate changes in molecular core conditions, as evidenced by the significant variability at 1665 MHz since 1993 and the changing velocity ranges of both 1665 and 1667 MHz emissions [1][2]. The 1665-MHz emission is weaker than in previous observations, covering a velocity range of 66 to at least 75 km/s, while the 1667-MHz emission is weak but spans a wider velocity range, from 64 to 84 km/s across an absorption feature [2]. The strongest 1665-MHz emission is accompanied by weaker emission at 1667 MHz at similar velocities, and both emissions are wholly right-hand circularly polarized (RHCP), suggesting that they may share the same regions of the OH shell [3][4]. The increase in the ratio of 1667 MHz emission to 1665 MHz emission is consistent with the expected evolution of maser emission in the post-AGB stage, where 1667 MHz emission becomes relatively stronger and eventually dominant [4].

The immune system is a complex collection of organs, tissues and cells which is present in all vertebrates and protects the organism from external pathogens . In this work we introduce a minimal model to describe the primary response of the adaptive immune system, a network of highly specialised cells that produces a targeted reaction to specific antigens, i.e. viruses. The main players are B and T cells, two different types of lymphocytes. They independently recognise the antigen binding it with their receptors (fig. REF ). Each group of T and B cells sharing the same receptors' structure (clone) is able to recognise and fight only a particular virus with complementary epitope.The immune response by B cells is activated or suppressed according to a confirmation signal sent by T cells in the form of excitatory or inhibitory proteins, the cytokines. Such response (when activated) consists in the secretion of antibodies, proteins able to chemically bind and neutralise the antigen, hence (possibly) avoiding the propagation of the infection.
This two- signals mechanism prevents erroneous B cells activations against mismatching antigens or other cells of the organism.In recent years, this system composed by a large number of interacting agents - T, B cells and antigens - has been looked at through the prism of statistical mechanics to understand its global features and functionalities, .

In particular, we study the effect of having B cells with a variable number of receptors on their surfaces, one of the most important mechanisms preventing autoimmune reactions and diseases:
a receptor editing process is indeed very commonly observed during the B cell maturation, where self-reactive cells, which may be responsible for the onset of autoimmune responses, are suppressed at an early stage of the development by changing the number of receptors .
We also introduce interactions between B cells, the so-called idiotypic network, first hypothesised by Jerne : B cells receptors can not only recognise antigens but also other B cells with complementary receptors. In the presence of an antigen antibodies with complementary receptors, called idiotypes and denoted with Ab1, are produced and recognised by complementary antibodies (Ab2) which share structural features with the original antigen.
According to recent experimental studies, the idiotypic network seems to play a central role in autoimmune diseases, supporting a cascade of autoantibodies production, which recognise each other and modulate the immune response.

We analyse the system's behaviour in different regions of the parameter's space (i.e. number of clones and triggered receptors, noise level, etc.) through linear stability analysis and Monte Carlo
simulations.

original contract's address or disrupting the network's trust.
Various design patterns enable upgradability,
such as proxy pattern, data separation pattern, and metamorphic
contracts . The most commonly used one is the proxy pattern, where a proxy
contract delegates calls to an implementation contract. This setup allows the implementations of
upgradable smart contracts to be effectively replaced in certain setter functions,
transparently upgrading contract's logic that does not change the original proxy contract address.
With contract upgrades, developers can perform bug fixes, introduce new functionality, or improve existing contract features.

In the context of EG models, semidirect products are used to construct models for infinite cyclic extensions of groups, whereas direct products are not typically used for this purpose. The semidirect product construction allows for the creation of a model for EG from a model for EB, provided that certain conditions are satisfied, such as the subgroup acting freely by conjugation on the set of conjugacy classes of non-trivial elements of B. input: How can Trajectory Stochastic Unit and C-VAE be combined to improve the accuracy of hand trajectory and interaction hotspot predictions in human-computer interaction models?
expected_output: The Trajectory Stochastic Unit and C-VAE can be combined to improve the accuracy of hand trajectory and interaction hotspot predictions in human-computer interaction models by introducing appropriate uncertainties to the final prediction results. Specifically, the Trajectory Stochastic Unit can be used to model the uncertainty in hand trajectories, while the C-VAE can be used to model the uncertainty in interaction hotspots. By incorporating both units into a deep network, the model can jointly predict future hand trajectories and interaction hotspots, achieving superior performance in anticipating interaction intentions. The C-VAE can be used as a network head in the Transformer decoder to model the uncertainty in prediction, and the Trajectory Stochastic Unit can be used to enhance the coherence between hand trajectories and interaction hotspots. This combination has been shown to achieve state-of-the-art results across three benchmark datasets, including Epic-Kitchens-100, EGO4D, and EGTEA Gaze+, demonstrating superior performance in complex scenarios.
actual_output: The Trajectory Stochastic Unit and C-VAE can be combined to improve the accuracy of hand trajectory and interaction hotspot predictions by introducing appropriate uncertainty to trajectories and interaction hotspots, respectively [1]. Conditioning C-VAE on hand trajectory improves interaction hotspot prediction performance compared to conditioning on contact points, and C-VAE achieves better results compared to Bivariate and MDN models for trajectory and contact point prediction [2]. The Trajectory Stochastic Unit calculates uncertain regions using intersecting ellipses based on hand positions at consecutive time steps and image dimensions, which can be used in conjunction with C-VAE to capture multi-modal distributions of trajectories and improve overall performance [3][4]. Using C-VAE with conditional dependencies between hand trajectory and object contact points further improves overall performance, demonstrating the benefits of combining these approaches for human-computer interaction models [5].

input: How can structural nested failure time models estimate causal effects of time-varying treatments, and what are the key considerations for their application in real-world scenarios?
expected_output: Structural nested failure time models can estimate the causal effects of time-varying treatments by explicitly accounting for time-dependent confounding, which occurs when patient characteristics that are themselves time-dependent influence both the treatment and the outcome of interest. These models are particularly useful in observational studies where the treatment may have been repeatedly adapted to patient characteristics, making it challenging to estimate the treatment effect by simply conditioning on these characteristics. The key considerations for applying structural nested failure time models in real-world scenarios include carefully defining the estimands of interest, such as the effect of a time-varying treatment on time to an event, and ensuring that the models are properly specified to capture the complex relationships between the treatment, patient characteristics, and the outcome. Additionally, it is essential to consider the potential for untestable assumptions and to conduct sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of the findings, as the treatment effect may not be fully identifiable without relying on such assumptions. By addressing these considerations, structural nested failure time models can provide a powerful tool for estimating the causal effects of time-varying treatments in a variety of settings.
actual_output: Structural nested failure time models (SNFTM) are designed to estimate the causal effect of a time-varying treatment on time to an event of interest in the presence of time-dependent confounding variables [1]. Section: Discussion

In this paper, we propose a novel multi-view learning method to explore the problem of multi-view clustering, called Locality Relationship Constrained Multi-view Clustering Framework (LRC-MCF). LRC-MCF attempts to capture the relationship information among samples under the constraint of locality structure and integrate the relationship from different views into one common similarity relationships matrix. Moreover, LRC-MCF provide an adaptive weight allocation mechanism to take sufficient consideration of the importance of different views in finding the common-view similarity relationships. To effectually reduce the redundancy of the learned representations, the low-rank constraint on the common similarity matrix is additionally considered. Correspondingly, this paper provides an algorithm based on the alternating direction minimization strategy to iteratively calculate all variables of LRC-MCF. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on seven benchmark multi-view datasets to validate the performance of LRC-MCF, and the experimental results show that the proposed LRC-MCF outperforms its counterparts and achieves comparable performance. input: What causes the variation in core accretion rates due to differences in grain growth and vaporization timescales?
expected_output: The variation in core accretion rates is caused by differences in grain growth and vaporization timescales, which determine whether grains can grow to a sufficient size before vaporizing, allowing them to sediment and contribute to core formation. Specifically, the grain growth timescale and the vaporization timescale of the grains are the key factors that influence the core accretion rate, with rapid grain growth and slower vaporization timescales leading to more efficient core formation. Additionally, parameters such as turbulent mixing, grain shattering by collisions, and the initial grain mass fraction also play a role in determining the core accretion rate.
actual_output: The variation in core accretion rates due to differences in grain growth and vaporization timescales is influenced by both accretion and coagulation, which are important processes in grain growth within the cores [1]. Accretion rates depend on the size of the core and increase cubically until the expansion wave leaves the core, then fall steadily, which can be affected by grain growth via accretion and coagulation [2][1]. The timescale of accretion is set by the cooling timescale of the inner convective zone of the envelope, and neglecting accretion rate variations can result in a significant underestimate of certain astrophysical processes [3][4]. Additionally, the accretion rate is modified by a factor related to the relative velocity for different core masses, and mass accretion rate onto the core is regulated by the energy dissipation of the incoming flow near the core [5][6].

input: What role do mass ratios play in determining the stability of central configurations, and how do different configurations respond to variations in mass ratios?
expected_output: The mass ratios play a crucial role in determining the stability of central configurations, as they uniquely define the configuration when the mutual distances satisfy certain conditions. According to the Dziobek equations, the mass ratios are given by specific formulas that are consistent with each other, and these formulas explain why a particular equation is sufficient for obtaining a central configuration. For configurations with unequal masses, the mass ratios determine the shape and orientation of the configuration, as seen in the equilateral solution where the mass ratios uniquely determine the configuration. In contrast, for configurations with equal masses, the configuration is indefinite, and any configuration with a specific angular relationship satisfies the equation of motion. The response of different configurations to variations in mass ratios is also significant, as changes in mass ratios can result in different configurations, such as the transition from an equilateral to an isosceles configuration. Overall, the mass ratios are a key factor in determining the stability and characteristics of central configurations.
actual_output: Mass ratios play a crucial role in determining the stability of central configurations, as they affect the force due to gravity on each body and its proportionality factor with respect to the center of mass [1]. The variation of mass ratios with certain parameters, such as energy levels, can be weak and may become even weaker with increasing values, as observed in the evolution of mass ratios below 1TeV, 2TeV, and 10 TeV for different cases [2][3]. Different configurations respond to variations in mass ratios in distinct ways, with the fraction of time in the high state being a strong function of mass ratio and temperature, and disk mass predictions changing as the mass ratio changes [4][5]. The study of central configurations and mass ratios is important for understanding the behavior of systems with moderate particle mass differences, although the global structure for very large differences in particle masses remains to be determined [6][7].

input: How does vaccine efficacy compare to vaccination rate in terms of reducing disease transmission, and what are the key differences in their impact on population health?
expected_output: Vaccine efficacy and vaccination rate are two distinct factors that play a crucial role in reducing disease transmission and impacting population health. According to the context, vaccine efficacy is the most determinant factor in reducing disease transmission, as illustrated in the figure where the effective vaccine is shown to have a significant impact on the cumulative force of infection. In contrast, the vaccination rate parameter has a marginal effect when the vaccine is not effective. However, when the vaccine parameter is low, the degree of disease reduction depends on the vaccination rate parameter, indicating that both factors are important in this scenario. The key difference in their impact on population health is that vaccine efficacy directly affects the ability of the vaccine to prevent infection, whereas vaccination rate influences the proportion of the population that is protected. Overall, the context suggests that a highly effective vaccine is essential for significantly reducing disease transmission, and a high vaccination rate can further enhance this effect, especially when vaccine efficacy is low.
actual_output: Vaccine efficacy and vaccination rate both play crucial roles in reducing disease transmission, with vaccine efficacy defined as the opposite of the relative risk among vaccinated individuals, and vaccination rate affecting the proportion of the population that is immune [1][2]. The efficiency of a vaccine can be defined in terms of reducing the risk of infection, the severity of the disease, or the duration of infectivity, and vaccine efficacies vary widely, ranging from 8% to 93% depending on vaccine type, year, and study population [3][1]. Higher vaccine efficacy significantly enhances vaccination coverage, especially in scale-free networks where highly connected hubs facilitate rapid vaccination spread, and even with imperfect vaccines and low coverage, a reduced transmission rate allows vaccines to prevent infection spread [4][5]. The impact of vaccine efficacy on disease transmission is further influenced by factors such as population turnover, which determines the epidemiological dynamics, and the basic reproduction number (ℛ₀), which is affected by vaccination coverage and vaccine efficiency [6][7].
